# ModForge editor text: English
#
# Every word the editor shows is here, one text per line: key = text.
# A translation is a copy of this file with the text after each = in another
# language, named for that language: es.txt, pt-BR.txt, zh-Hans.txt...
# Language > New or update a translation, in the editor, writes one for you
# to start from.
# The texts under [In the game] are the ones the game shows players; the
# rest is the editor. One file does both: put it in the editor's languages
# folder, and in the game's BepInEx\plugins\SMSModForge\Languages folder.
#
# Lines starting with # are notes, and [headings] only help you find your way.
# Neither changes anything.
# Keep {words in braces}, <tags> and [TOKENS:like this] exactly as they are:
# something fills them in or reads them.
# \n starts a new line. An underscore marks the letter Alt reaches a menu by.
# Nothing after the = shows the English. "" shows nothing, on purpose.
# A key ending in .one or .other is one form of a sentence with a number in it.
# A translation has the forms its own language uses; ModForge writes them out.

[This file]

# The language's name, written the way its speakers write it
language.name = English

# yes for a machine translation nobody has checked yet
language.machineTranslated = no

# Who made or checked this translation
language.translators =

action.setVariable.name.tip = Pack variable to set.

# Label beside a field of an action or condition
param.label.value = Value

# Tooltip on the 'Value' field of the SetVariable action
action.setVariable.value.tip = New value. Strings round-trip as-is; use 'true' / 'false' for booleans, and numbers in invariant-culture form (e.g. '3.14'). '$varName' copies that variable's current value instead ('$$' escapes a literal dollar). Leave it blank to CLEAR the variable to an empty string — that's kept as a real value, not treated as an unfilled row.

# Tooltip on the 'Variable' field of the IncrementVariable action
action.incrementVariable.name.tip = Numeric pack variable to add to (negative delta subtracts).

# Label beside a field of an action or condition
param.label.delta = Delta

# Tooltip on the 'Delta' field of the IncrementVariable action
action.incrementVariable.delta.tip = Amount added to the current value each time the action runs.

# Label beside a field of an action or condition
param.label.focused = Focused

# Tooltip on the 'Focused' field of the CharacterFocus action
action.setSpriteFocus.focused.tip = When true, every actor's bust in the dialogue is bumped above the CG layer; when false, their resting sorting orders are restored. No per-actor target — it focuses the whole cast, and resets automatically when the dialogue ends.

param.label.actor = Actor

# Tooltip on the 'Actor' field of the LeaveBust action

# Tooltip on the 'GO path' field of the SetGameObjectActive action

# Label beside a field of an action or condition
param.label.active = Active

action.setGameObjectActive.active.tip = true to switch the target on, false to switch it off, or toggle to flip it to the opposite of whatever it currently is. Toggle reads the object's own state, so a parent being hidden around it does not count as off.

# Label beside a field of an action or condition
param.label.property = Property

# Tooltip on the 'Property' field of the SetComponentProperty action
action.setComponentProperty.property.tip = Which field to set. CanvasGroup: 'alpha' hides the whole UI subtree without deactivating it (so anything animating underneath keeps running); 'interactable' turns its controls on or off; 'blocksRaycasts' decides whether clicks stop here or pass through to what is behind. Hiding a panel usually wants all three, which is three rows.

# Tooltip on the 'Value' field of the SetComponentProperty action
action.setComponentProperty.value.tip = The new value, read to suit the property: a number for 'alpha' (0..1), 'true' / 'false' for the two flags.

# Tooltip on the 'Duration (s)' field of the SetComponentProperty action
action.setComponentProperty.seconds.tip = 0 sets the value immediately; anything higher tweens to it. Numeric properties only — a flag has nothing to tween through, so this is ignored for those and the change lands at once.

# Label beside a field of an action or condition

# Tooltip on the 'Chance' field of the Random condition
condition.random.chance.tip = DEPRECATED — re-rolls on EVERY evaluation. In a per-frame context (integration rule, dialogue start conditions, button visibility) that means ~60 rolls/second and the probability is meaningless. Switch to 'DailyChance' (once per day) or a LevelRandom variable + comparison.

# Tooltip on the 'Chance' field of the DailyChance condition
condition.dailyChance.chance.tip = Probability of passing, as a whole percentage. 50 = passes on ~half of in-game days. Rolled once per in-game day: the result holds all day, survives save/reload, and changes at each day roll-over. Every DailyChance rolls independently — the console names each one after its dialogue/rule at the day change.

# Tooltip on "_Spell-check node text"
menu.spellCheckNodeText.tip = Underline misspellings using Windows' own spell checker, in the language the lines are written in - the pack's own, or the one you are editing in - both in a node's Text field and down the node list, so mistakes are visible while scanning. A language Windows has no spelling dictionary for is not underlined at all; Windows' language settings can add one. Right-click a squiggle in the Text field for suggestions, to ignore it for this session, or to add the word to your Windows dictionary (the same list Edge and Office use). Turning this off also makes the node list lighter to scroll on very long dialogues. Your choice is remembered between sessions.

# Tooltip on "Smart _suggestions in dropdowns"
menu.smartSuggestions.tip = When you open an empty dropdown, the options that what you are editing makes likely move to the top, marked with a star: in a dialogue that mentions a character anywhere and happens at one place, a Set Active action lists that character's scenes at that place first. Everything in the dialogue, scene or rule you have up counts - the characters it names, its places, its variables, the folder it is in - and it follows your edits as you make them. Nothing is picked or hidden for you, and other dropdowns showing the same list keep their own order. Turn this off to have every list in its usual order.

# Tooltip on "_Version the pack automatically"
menu.versionPackAutomatically.tip = Move the pack's version on every save: up a minor when the pack gains something, up a patch when something it already had changes. The major number is never moved for you — that one says "this is a new version of the pack", which is yours to decide. Off means the version only ever changes when you type it.

# Tooltip on "Warn when the version goes _backwards"
menu.warnWhenVersionGoes.tip = Ask before saving a version lower than the one already on disk. Going backwards is nearly always a typo, and it makes a new release read as older than the copy a player already has.

# Tooltip on "Warn about _large exports"
menu.warnAboutLargeExports.tip = Ask before exporting a pack folder over 150 MB or 1600 files, in case it has swept up something that is not part of the pack. Unticking clears the per-pack "don't warn again" you may have set from the prompt itself.
# Tooltip on "Offer to _translate before exporting"
menu.offerTranslationOnExport.tip = Before an export or a publish, when some of what players read in this pack is not yet in every language ModForge has, offer to translate it by machine. Only what is still untranslated is sent. For this pack only.

# Tooltip on "Add pack _names to Windows dictionary…"

# Box heading
places.placeGameObjects = GameObjects (this place's scene hierarchy)

# Text
places.everythingPlaceBuildsUnder = Everything this place builds under its level, as one hierarchy. A GameObject with a Sprite is a layered sprite object (backdrop, prop, animated layer); leave the Sprite blank for a pure container that just groups children. Every node takes utility components (fade, disappear, random child, blink), nested children, and NPC placements. The NPCs node is the level's own NPCs object — always present, and the home for the NPC hierarchy; its subtree composes local transforms down the chain, so moving a container moves everything under it. Target any node from dialogue by Name with SetGameObjectActive / FadeSprite / MoveGameObject / SpinGameObject. Lower sorting draws further back.

Convention: asterisk-bracketed lowercase tokens like *plap*, *smooch*. One SFX can carry multiple patterns — *yank*,*yeet* both fire the same clip just like the host mod does. # Box heading
integration.repeatEachOptional = Repeat for each (optional)

# Text
integration.runsWholeRuleOnce = Runs this whole rule once per value, so one rule can cover a set of subjects instead of copying it per subject. Values: a comma-separated list (A,B,C), or $variableName naming a List variable (or a String variable holding CSV) — so the set can change at runtime. Each value is substituted wherever {name} appears in any condition or action, including branches: e.g. Location_{char} as a variable name, or {char}/Slot as a GameObject path. It composes with the rest of the syntax — $Prefix_{char} dereferences the per-value variable. Every value gets its own edge state and its own Timer deadlines, so values behave exactly like the separate rules they replace (tick 'stagger' on a Timer to spread their first fire apart). Leave blank to run the rule once.

integration.eachValue = For each value in:

# Box heading

# Text
integration.editRuleSTrigger = Edit the rule's trigger mode + conditions + actions as a JSON object. Format: { "triggerMode": "OnRisingEdge", "conditions": [...], "actions": [...], "branches": [ { "conditions": [...], "actions": [...] } ] }. branches is the optional else-if chain (first match wins; empty conditions = plain Else). The conditions / actions arrays carry the same shape as dialogue nodes' actionsOnStart.

# Tooltip on a tick box
ui.fitToContent.tip = With a set number of columns, the grid is only as wide as the columns its objects fill - two objects in a grid of eight columns make it two cells wide - so something sized to the grid, like a Content Size Fitter, grows and shrinks with what it holds. With a set number of rows, the same for its height. Unity's own grid is always as wide as all its columns. Only in the game: the preview draws the grid at its own size.

# Tooltip on a text box

# Tooltip on a dropdown

# Tooltip on a dropdown
ui.textmeshproFontAssetNot.tip = A TextMeshPro font asset, not a font file. The same typeface appears more than once with different outlines and shadows, and they are not interchangeable.

[Docs: What a mod pack is]

# Docs: a topic's title
docs.modPack.title = What a mod pack is

# Docs: the line under the topic's title
docs.modPack.summary = The whole idea, before any of the detail.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.modPack.packOneFolderEverything = A pack is one folder. Everything you author ends up in a single file inside it called modpack.json, and the images and audio sit beside that file.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.modPack.neverEditModpackJson = You never edit modpack.json by hand. The editor writes it, and its tabs are the things it can hold.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.modPack.exportTurnsFolderInto = Export turns the folder into one .smspack file. That is what you hand to players, and the only thing the game reads.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.modPack.gameDoesNotKnow = The game does not know the editor exists. It reads your pack through the SMSModForge plugin, which is what actually builds your characters, rooms and conversations inside the running game.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic
docs.modPack.heading.worthKnowing = Worth knowing

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.modPack.packAddsGameRather = A pack adds to the game rather than replacing it. Your places sit alongside the game's own, and a vanilla extension adds to a room the game already has instead of swapping it out.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.modPack.nothingDoEditorTouches = Nothing you do in the editor touches your game installation until you export and copy the pack in yourself.

[Docs: The order to work in]

# Docs: the line under the topic's title

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.orderWork.fileThenNewPack.term = First

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.orderWork.fileThenNewPack = File then New pack, and Save straight away. Previews and file pickers resolve paths against the pack folder, so much of the editor stays empty until that folder exists on disk.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.orderWork.charactersThenNpcsCharacter.term = Who

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.orderWork.charactersThenNpcsCharacter = Characters, then NPCs. A character can speak; an NPC just stands in a room. Both want their art before anything else can point at them.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.orderWork.placesThenMapButtons.term = Where

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.orderWork.placesThenMapButtons = Places, then Map Buttons. A place is a room. A map button is how a player reaches one.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.orderWork.dialoguesDialogueBelongsLevel.term = What they say

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.orderWork.dialoguesDialogueBelongsLevel = Dialogues. A dialogue belongs to a level and its lines name characters, so both are worth having first.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.orderWork.scenesMusicSFXWallpapers.term = What plays

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.orderWork.scenesMusicSFXWallpapers = Scenes, Music, SFX and Wallpapers. These are things a dialogue or a rule can trigger, so add them before the logic that fires them.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.orderWork.variablesThenIntegrationVariable.term = State and logic

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.orderWork.variablesThenIntegrationVariable = Variables, then Integration. A variable has to exist before a condition or an action can name it.

docs.maskPainter.fileItselfCharacterMask = In the file itself a character mask keeps Bounce, Wave and Noise in the red, green and blue channels with alpha scaling all three, and a place mask keeps its one layer in alpha alone. That only matters if you ever paint a mask in another program — here it is handled for you.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.optionsMenu.underlineMisspellingsNodeS.term = Spell-check node text

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.optionsMenu.underlineMisspellingsNodeS = Underline misspellings in a node's Text field and down the node list, using the same US-English checker Windows uses elsewhere. Right-click a squiggle for suggestions, to ignore the word for this session, or to add it to your Windows dictionary. Switching it off also makes very long node lists lighter to scroll.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.optionsMenu.addEveryCharacterPlace.term = Add pack names to Windows dictionary…

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.optionsMenu.addEveryCharacterPlace = Add every character, place and NPC name the pack invents to your Windows dictionary at once, so they stop being flagged. Shows you the list before adding anything.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.optionsMenu.tradePreviewSmoothnessAgainst.term = Preview quality

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.optionsMenu.tradePreviewSmoothnessAgainst = Choose how much of the game's look the previews draw, against processor load. Every quality draws as many frames as your display shows. Ultra is the game's own picture: the edge glow, bloom, light streaks and colour. High leaves out the light streaks, and on the processor works the edge glow out more quickly, without the bust's shadow in it; Medium leaves out the bloom too; Low the edge glow as well. With no backdrop the qualities save work too: Ultra draws a bust or an NPC as finely as the game does on a large screen, High with half the work, Medium a quarter, and Low one point for every four pixels.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.optionsMenu.previewBackdrop.term = Preview backdrop

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.optionsMenu.previewBackdrop = What the bust preview draws a bust over. The PC's room, the default, shows it as the game does there: the room behind, the light of its lamps, the glow its edges take from the room, and its breathing moving it over the room. The Beach, the Forest, the Villa and the Temple do the same in four more of the game's places, each with its own look. None shows the bust alone. The Backdrop buttons at the bottom of the Characters tab are the same setting, and the mask painter's preview follows it too.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.optionsMenu.previewRenderer.term = Draw previews on

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.optionsMenu.previewRenderer = What draws the live previews. Automatic, the default, times the graphics card and the processor when the editor starts and uses the faster. On the graphics card the previews run the game's own programs; the first time, it takes a few seconds to prepare them.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic
docs.optionsMenu.heading.worthKnowing = Worth knowing

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.optionsMenu.windowsDictionarySharedRest = The Windows dictionary is shared with the rest of your system, so words added here also stop being flagged in other apps that use it.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.dialogues.gameChecksBeforePlays.term = The game plays this when

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.dialogues.gameChecksBeforePlays = What the game checks before it plays the conversation, one group per place that plays it - any one of them is enough. Take out removes one of the game's conditions from that place's script; it stays listed, struck through, with Put back beside it. The script is the room's, not the conversation's, so anything else it guards - another conversation, a quest it starts - happens without the condition too, and the Quests tab shows the same change. Where the place is (the room it belongs to) cannot be taken out here - a conversation is always played somewhere; a quest's place on the Quests tab can. A room tries its conversations in order and plays the first one that can, so the ones it says it tries first still come before this one, whatever you take out. Reset all puts these back as well.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.dialogues.lineOneGameS.term = Saves under way

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.dialogues.lineOneGameS = A line of one of the game's conversations that you change, add or take out can set or skip something the game's story needs, so it can break a save already under way - and removing your pack later can too. The Dialogues tab says so in orange. The first time a player loads an existing save with a pack that does this, the game warns them and recommends a new game; new games are not warned. A conversation you picked but left as the game has it changes nothing and is not warned about.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.dialogues.wherePlayGoesAfter.term = Then

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.dialogues.wherePlayGoesAfter = Where play goes after this node. Continue, the default, moves to the next node down the list — whether that is a child of this one or something further out. Exit stops the conversation and skips everything below. Jump resumes at whichever node carries the tag you name. Once that node and the lines under it are done, the game says again any line it is under, then that line's lines - so a jump that lands under the very line that jumps goes round for ever. A node at the top level carries on cleanly, and Validate warns about the others.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.dialogues.veryBottomDialogueContinue = At the very bottom of a dialogue, Continue and Exit do the same thing, because there is nothing left to skip either way. Exit only means something when something comes after it.

docs.quests.whenAllThemPass.term = Start conditions

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.whenAllThemPass = When all of them pass, the quest starts by itself and its first task with it. They are checked continuously, so they offer the same conditions a dialogue's start conditions do.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.noStartConditionsQuest.term = Empty

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.noStartConditionsQuest = With no start conditions the quest waits for a Quest action to start it. Unlike most condition lists, empty does not mean always.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic
docs.quests.heading.resetsWhen = Resets when

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.whenAllThemPass2.term = Reset conditions

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.whenAllThemPass2 = When all of them pass, a quest that has started - in progress, completed or failed - goes back to not started, its tasks and counts with it, so it can be done again. They are checked continuously. On your quests and on the game's.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.whileResetConditionsPass.term = Start conditions wait

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.whileResetConditionsPass = While the reset conditions pass, the start conditions are not asked, so a quest whose two lists both pass does not start and reset in turn.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.noResetConditionsQuest.term = Empty

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.noResetConditionsQuest = With no reset conditions the quest only goes back to not started when a Quest action resets it - or, for one of the game's, where the game does it.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic
docs.quests.heading.stepsAdded = Tasks added after players finished it

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.stepsAdded.leave.term = Leave it finished

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.stepsAdded.leave = The default. A player who had finished the quest keeps it finished and never sees the new tasks.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.stepsAdded.reopen.term = Reopen at the new steps

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.stepsAdded.reopen = The quest is in progress again the next time the player loads their save: every task they did stays done, and the first new task starts. Only when it is a clean addition - every new task comes after every task the quest already had, and the player had done all of those. Otherwise it stays finished, so nobody is stuck behind a task they cannot reach. A new choice under an "any one" task, or a note under a "by action" one, never reopens it.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.stepsAdded.startOver.term = Start it over

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.stepsAdded.startOver = The player's progress on the quest is cleared and it goes back to not started, so it starts again the way it always starts - its start conditions, or a Quest action. Each task's actions run again as it is done.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.stepsAdded.whichNew.term = Which tasks are new

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.stepsAdded.whichNew = ModForge remembers which tasks the quest had the last time each save was played with your pack. A save from before this was remembered has no record, so for it the tasks the player never did that come after the last one they did count as new. Only your own quests: one of the game's quests stays as the player left it.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic
docs.quests.heading.tasks = Tasks

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.topLevelTasksRun.term = Order

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.topLevelTasksRun = Top-level tasks run one after another. Starting the quest starts the first, finishing one starts the next, and finishing the last completes the quest.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.listedUnderTheirTask.term = Subtasks

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.listedUnderTheirTask = Listed under their task with a small arrow. The journal never ticks a subtask, finished or not; only top-level tasks get a check mark.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.questSDescriptionBecomes.term = Quest description once done

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.questSDescriptionBecomes = What the quest's description becomes once this task is done. Several tasks can have one: the journal shows the one from the task furthest down the list that is done, and the quest's own description before any of them is.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.subtaskJournalListsEvery.term = Hidden until it starts

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.subtaskJournalListsEvery = On a subtask. The journal lists every subtask of a task it shows, started or not; ticked, this one stays out of the journal until it starts - under a task whose subtasks run in order, once the subtask before it is done. A top-level task needs no tick: the journal already leaves one out until it starts.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.anyTaskKeepsOut.term = Hidden until conditions pass

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.anyTaskKeepsOut = On any task. Keeps it out of the journal until the conditions under it all pass. Once they have, it stays in the journal for the rest of that save - remembered with the save - unless 'Hide it again when they stop passing' is ticked, in which case it is shown only while they pass. With no conditions it is shown at once. Hiding a task changes nothing about when it or its quest finishes.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.taskSubtasksFinishesOrder.term = Completes

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.taskSubtasksFinishesOrder = How a task with subtasks finishes: in order (one subtask at a time), any order (all of them, started together), any one (the first one done), or by action. By action means its subtasks never start, so they read as notes under it.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.givesTaskCountReaching.term = Counts to

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.givesTaskCountReaching = Gives the task a count. Reaching the target completes the task. The journal only shows the count beside a top-level task.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.questActionQuestActions.term = Counted by

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.questActionQuestActions = Quest action: Quest actions set the count or add to it. Variable: the count follows a number variable - one of your pack's, or one of the game's - for as long as the task is in progress, and completes the task when the variable reaches the target.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.conditionsFinishTaskThemselves.term = Completes when

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.conditionsFinishTaskThemselves = Conditions that finish the task by themselves: while it is in progress, the moment all of them pass it is done. With none, only a Quest action or the counter finishes it.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.actionsRunTaskFinishes.term = When it completes

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.actionsRunTaskFinishes = Actions that run as the task finishes, however it was finished: by its conditions, by a Quest action anywhere in the pack, or by its counter.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.onlyTaskWithoutSubtasks = Only a task without subtasks has these two lists. A task with subtasks finishes through them, so its subtasks carry the conditions and actions instead.

The quest stays the game's; your pack changes what the journal shows of it, what happens as the player works through it, and - if you choose - which tasks it has. Everything it changes goes back to the game's own if your pack is removed.

# Docs: a point in the topic

The description has a Reset of its own. A task of the game's that you change is marked with a dot in the list; its panel lists each change with its own way back, and Reset puts the task back.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.gameSTasksGame = The game's tasks in the game's order, with yours among them marked 'yours'. Faded rows are hidden from the journal; struck-through ones are taken out of the quest.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.addsTopLevelTask.term = + Task

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.addsTopLevelTask = Adds a top-level task of yours just after the selected top-level task, or at the end. The game waits for it like any of its own: the tasks after it hold until it is done, and the quest does not finish without it.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.addsSubtaskYoursEnd.term = + Subtask

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.addsSubtaskYoursEnd = Adds a subtask of yours - at the end of the selected top-level task's subtasks, or just after the selected subtask. Works on the game's steps too, including one with no subtasks yet, which then finishes through its subtasks as the game does. Added tasks go two levels deep, as the game's do.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen

# Docs: a point in the topic

# Docs: a point in the topic

Quest actions and conditions name it on the Vanilla side, by the game's quest and its runtime name.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.oneGameSTasks.term = Take it out of the quest

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.oneGameSTasks = On one of the game's tasks. It is not deleted - the game's own scenes still name it - but hidden, with everything under it, and the quest moves past it the moment it starts, as though the game had completed it. Under a task that finishes with any one of its subtasks it is left alone instead, so it cannot finish that task by itself. Untick to put it back.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.oneGameSTasks2.term = In the journal

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.oneGameSTasks2 = On one of the game's tasks: shown as the game has it, hidden until conditions of yours pass (with the same 'Hide it again when they stop passing' choice a task of your own has), always hidden, or (for a subtask) hidden until it starts. Hiding a task changes nothing about when the quest finishes.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.actionsRunOnceMoment = Actions that run once, the moment the game marks one of its tasks done - by its own dialogue or by a Quest action of yours.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.conditionsStartGameS.term = Starts when

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.conditionsStartGameS = Conditions that start the game's quest early, if the game has not started it already. What the game does to start it normally is unchanged.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.readOnlyQuestEach.term = What the game does with it

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.readOnlyQuestEach = Read-only, on the quest and on each of its tasks: every place the game starts the quest or puts it back to not started, and every place it completes, counts, fails or abandons a task. Each says which conversation and line it is on (as the line appears, or once it is done) and the lines leading there, or which script on which object runs it and which conversations that script plays just before and after it, and what has to be true - the conditions on the way and what the conversation needs to play. A condition ModForge has no equivalent for is listed in the game's own words. A step on a task only takes effect while that task is in progress. Every quest step in the game is covered.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.placesUnderStartedPut.term = Changing a place

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.placesUnderStartedPut = On the places under Started by and Put back to not started by. Each of the game's conditions around the step is listed where it lives - a line on the way, the line itself, the place that plays the conversation, or the script. Take out removes one from the game (struck through, with Put back); a line's condition is taken out of your version of that conversation, a place's out of its script, and either way whatever else it guards happens without it too - the Dialogues tab shows the same change. Where the script sits is a row of its own and can be taken out as well. And only if (yours) adds conditions of your own. Once you change anything at a place, that place is yours: what is left - the game's conditions you kept, the room, and yours - is asked over and over, and the quest starts (or goes back to not started) the moment it all passes, whether or not the game's own conversation or script ever gets there. Take everything out and add a key press, and the key press starts it; take the room out too and it starts anywhere. A place you have not touched behaves as the game wrote it, and putting everything back gives it back to the game. A place also says which of the room's conversations the game tries first, which decides the conversation but not your rule, and the game's log says which one the room played. A changed place is marked with a dot, and its reset arrow puts it back the way the game has it. Places that complete, count or fail a task are shown, not changed.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.besidePlaceConversationShows.term = Open conversation

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.besidePlaceConversationShows = Beside a place in a conversation: shows that conversation on the Dialogues tab with the line selected. If your pack does not change it yet, you are asked before it is added to your vanilla conversations; it changes nothing until you edit it.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.everyTaskListGame.term = When a task starts

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.everyTaskListGame = Every task in the list, the game's and yours, says when it starts. Nothing starts a task directly; the quest's order does. The first top-level task starts with the quest and each one after it once the one before is done; a task whose subtasks run in order starts the first of them, one whose subtasks run in any order - or finish with any one - starts them all, and one completed by an action starts none. A task your pack takes out is skipped on the way.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.addingTakingOutTasks.term = Saves under way

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.addingTakingOutTasks = Adding or taking out tasks can leave a save that is part-way through the quest unable to finish it, and so can removing your pack later. The editor says so in orange on any entry that does it. The first time a player loads an existing save with such a pack, the game warns them, lists the quests whose tasks change with where their save is in each - not started, in progress, possibly stuck because a task was added before where they are, or already finished - and recommends a new game; new games are not warned. Changes to the game's conversations are warned about the same way - see Dialogues; changes to its places are not. A save that has progress on tasks a quest no longer has is put back on its feet once: the plugin completes steps whose subtasks are all done, starts the next step where nothing is in progress, and completes the quest when all its steps are.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.quests.loadingSaveHasData.term = Missing packs

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.loadingSaveHasData = Loading a save that has data from a pack that is not installed tells the player which pack, and that its data will not be carried into saves they make from then on.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic
docs.quests.heading.worthKnowing = Worth knowing

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.questNeedsNothingOutside = A quest needs nothing outside this tab to start, move along and finish. The Quest action and the QuestState and QuestCounter conditions let a dialogue, a rule or a button take part as well - see Actions and Conditions.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.gameOnlyFinishesTask = The game only finishes a task that is in progress. Completing a task the player has not reached yet does nothing, and says so in the game's log.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.finishingQuestGivesPlayer = Finishing a quest gives the player the same reward the game's own quests give.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.quests.playersProgressSavedUnder = Players' progress is saved under the runtime names of the quest and its tasks. Renaming either after release starts that quest over for everyone who has the pack.

docs.conditions.compareVariableAgainstValue.term = Variable

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.conditions.compareVariableAgainstValue = Compare a variable against a value. Source chooses between your pack's own variables and the game's; Comparison offers equals, greater than, greater or equal, less than, less or equal, and exists — which passes once the variable has been given any value at all.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.conditions.passesWhenTextVariable.term = VariableStartsWith

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.conditions.passesWhenTextVariable = Passes when a text variable begins with something. The one the comparisons above cannot express: where a value is compound, like a location built from a room and a spot in it, a prefix answers which room am I in without listing every spot.

# Docs: a point in the topic

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.conditions.gameReadsKeysPOSITION.term = Keyboard layouts

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.conditions.gameReadsKeysPOSITION = The game reads keys by POSITION, not by the letter printed on the cap — the key called A is wherever A sits on a US keyboard, which is Q on AZERTY. The picker groups the letters, number row and punctuation separately for that reason; mouse buttons, arrows, modifiers, function keys and the numpad sit in the same place everywhere and are the safe choice for anything a player has to be able to press.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.conditions.mostConditionsAvailableAnywhere = Most conditions are available anywhere a condition can be written.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.conditions.randomOfferedOnlyWhere = Random is offered only where a condition is checked once and then done with — a node's own conditions, and a place's enter and exit hooks. Anywhere that is checked continuously, a fresh roll every frame would flicker rather than decide, so DailyChance is the one to reach for.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.conditions.timerOfferedOnlyIntegration = Timer is offered only on integration rules, because it measures from the last time the rule fired and nothing else has a moment like that.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.conditions.inputkeyOfferedEverywhereBut = InputKey is offered everywhere, but its two edge phases — Pressed and Released — are only meaningful where a condition is re-checked continuously. On a node's own conditions, which are checked once when the conversation reaches the node, Validate warns and points you at Down or Up.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic

Opening such a pack rewrites each of them to the matching Variable type with Source set to Vanilla, so they will not survive the next save and there is no reason to write a new one.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.targetPicker.objectsStartSwitchedOff = Objects that start switched off are still found, so an action can turn on something that was never visible.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.targetPicker.targetResolvesNothingReported = A target that resolves to nothing is reported in the game's log rather than stopping anything, so a mistyped name shows up as an action that quietly does nothing.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.targetPicker.conditionThereNoLog = In a condition there is no log line for it: an object that cannot be found reads the same as one switched off. Negate therefore means off or absent, not off — so a mistyped target in a negated condition passes rather than complaining.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen

# Docs: a point in the topic

Click one to see the English and write your own words for it - a text that says a number shows each form the language uses. Saved in your languages folder and shown at once. Texts in menus, messages and tooltips have no pencil: Find a text to edit searches all of them by their words.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.files.term = Translation files

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.files = One text file per language, named for it: es.txt, pt-BR.txt, zh-Hans.txt. Each line is key = text, with the English it was translated from in a note above it. Any text editor opens one, and a Replace All in Notepad++ is safe: Check a translation finds the keys it changed and puts them back.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.newOrUpdate.term = New or update a translation…

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.newOrUpdate = Writes a file of your own to start from, in your languages folder, or brings yours up to date after an update of the editor: new texts arrive in English, changed ones are marked 'changed from', and nothing you wrote is lost.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.check.term = Check a translation…

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.check = Lists what is missing, broken or out of date, line by line: a {gap}, a <tag> or a count form lost in translation, a line the editor cannot read.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.sharing.term = Passing one on

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.sharing = Send the file. Whoever gets it puts it in their languages folder (Language ▸ Open my languages folder), and it appears in their Language menu. A file there is laid over the one that came with the editor: its words show wherever it has some for the English as it is now, and the editor's own translation everywhere else - so an update of the editor still brings its new texts, and never touches the file.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic

# Docs: a point in the topic

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.editingIn.term = Editing in

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.editingIn = Beside the tabs: pick a language to see the whole pack in it - lines, names, quests, buttons - and edit it right where you edit your own words. What you type goes into that language's file and your own words stay as they are; saving writes both, and lists the translation's changes with the rest.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.translatePack.term = Translate the pack…

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.translatePack = File ▸ Pack translations ▸ Translate the pack…: translates by machine (Google) whatever is still untranslated, into the languages you tick. Characters' names are kept as they are and spelled in each language's own alphabet - Google suggests, and you check, before anything is translated - and the pronouns you gave your characters tell it who says each line. Everything a machine writes is marked, and Editing in corrects any of it.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.packFile.term = Pack translations

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.packFile = File ▸ Pack translations ▸ New or update a translation… writes translations/<code>.txt in the pack's folder, with every text a player reads: lines and choices, character names, quest titles, descriptions and tasks, navigator and world map buttons, and the texts on your screens. Each has a note saying where it appears. The folder goes into the exported pack.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.ai.term = With an AI tool

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.ai = Give it the whole file and ask it to translate only the text after each =, changing nothing else. Save what it gives back in place of the file, then run File ▸ Pack translations ▸ Check the pack's translations: it finds any key, gap, tag or [PV:...] token that did not come back as it went.

# Docs: the bold label in front of the next text, usually a name on screen
docs.translations.players.term = What players see

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.players = A player whose game is set to that language gets the pack in it, with nothing to set up. A line you change after it was translated shows your new words until the translation is brought up to date, never an old translation of something else.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic
docs.translations.heading.game = In the game

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.setting = The plugin's Language setting, in BepInEx\config\treboy.starmakerstory.smsmodforge.packplugin.cfg, picks the language for ModForge's own words and for every pack. auto follows the language Windows is set to.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.fonts = The game itself is in English and stays so. Its fonts only draw Latin letters, so for Chinese, Japanese, Korean or Russian the plugin puts Windows' own font for that language behind them.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.gameWords = ModForge's own words in the game - the pack list on the main menu, the save warning - come from the same translation file as the editor's, under [In the game]. Put the file in BepInEx\plugins\SMSModForge\Languages and players see them in that language.

# Docs: a heading inside the topic
docs.translations.heading.worthKnowing = Worth knowing

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.machine = Translations that came with the editor were made by a machine, and say so in the Language menu until somebody checks them. Corrections are welcome: make them with Edit texts on screen, or in the file, and pass the file on.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.storedStays = What a pack stores does not change with the language: keys, names you gave things and the values conditions compare stay as you typed them.

# Docs: a point in the topic
docs.translations.variables = Text you put into a variable and show with [PV:...] is not translated: it is data, and a condition may be comparing it.

tutorial.firstSteps.startFreshPack.title = Start a fresh pack

# Tutorials: what the step says

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstSteps.saveSomewhere.title = Save it somewhere

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstSteps.saveSomewhere.body = Use File then Save, and make a NEW empty folder for it — not your Desktop or Documents. A pack owns its whole folder: everything inside ends up in the exported file. Saving here also matters because previews and file pickers resolve paths against that folder, and stay empty until there is one.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.firstSteps.saveSomewhere.hint = File then Save, or Ctrl+S. Make a new folder rather than reusing one.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstSteps.giveThemFace.title = Give them a face

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstSteps.giveThemFace.body = Every character needs at least one outfit, and every outfit needs a base sprite: the picture of them from the chest up. Point this one at one of the five practice busts. They live in TutorialArt/Busts, one folder each, and the base picture is the file whose name ends in Base00 — so Bust1 is TutorialArt/Busts/Bust1/Bust1Base00.png, and Bust2 through Bust5 follow the same pattern.\n\nAny of them works here. They differ in shape on purpose, which will matter when you paint a jiggle mask later; the fuller ones give you more to see. The other files in those folders are the blink, mouth and expression art, and a later tutorial uses them.\n\nBust art is 256 by 256 pixels, PNG, with a transparent background. Other sizes are scaled to fit rather than refused, but 256 is the only size whose pixels land exactly as you drew them, and anything that is not square gets transparent bars on two sides. When you come to draw your own, that is the shape to draw.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.firstSteps.giveThemFace.hint = Use the Browse button beside Base, under Sprites.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstSteps.thereThey.title = There they are

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstSteps.thereThey.body = The preview draws the bust the way the game will, and keeps up as you work — worth watching rather than exporting to find out.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstSteps.sayOutfitHas.title = Say what this outfit has

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstSteps.sayOutfitHas.body = A bust can carry more than its base picture: a blink frame, four mouth frames that animate while it talks, and four expressions. The three tickboxes are how you DECLARE which of those exist — they are not features to switch on, they are you telling the game what art to go looking for.\n\nYou are not using any of them yet, so untick all three: Has Blink frame, Has Mouth frames, Has Expressions. Getting this wrong is worth understanding now, because it fails silently — a ticked box with no art behind it reads as a BROKEN outfit, and the game skips the whole character rather than skipping the blink. A missing character with no error is almost always this.\n\nLeave Mask empty. An empty mask means the bust does not move, which is a perfectly good answer and the one you want until you paint one.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.firstSteps.sayOutfitHas.hint = Two tickboxes in the Sprites box, one in Expressions just below it.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstSteps.pack.title = That is a pack

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstSteps.pack.body = Save it, and File then Export pack bundles the folder into a single .smspack — the file the game loads. Drop that into the Mods folder in your game folder, beside the game's .exe, and it is installed.\n\nExport is the quick loop, for trying your own work in the game. Use it as often as you like: it changes nothing about the pack itself.\n\nThere is nothing to see in the game yet, because a character only appears once something gives them a line.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstSteps.givingSomebodyElse.title = Giving it to somebody else

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstSteps.givingSomebodyElse.body = File then Publish for players is the other end of that. It checks the pack over first and says so if anything is broken, then writes a zip holding one thing: your pack, already sitting in a Mods folder. Whoever downloads it extracts that into their game folder and is finished — there is no step left for them to get wrong, which is where most mods are lost. Nothing else is in the archive, so installing two packs never asks anybody to overwrite anything.\n\nIt opens the folder it wrote to afterwards, so the file is never somewhere you have to go looking for.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstSteps.writtenIn.title = The language it is written in

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstSteps.writtenIn.body = Written in, on this tab, says which language your pack's own words are in. It matters once the pack is translated: translations are made from it, and a player whose language has no translation reads the pack in it.\n\nWhen you export or publish, ModForge offers to translate by machine whatever is not yet in every language it has. Only what is still untranslated is sent, and a line you corrected yourself stays as you wrote it. To read or correct a translation, pick its language under Editing in, at the right end of the tabs, and edit as usual — it is saved with the pack.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstSteps.numberBesidePack.title = The number beside your pack

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstSteps.numberBesidePack.body = Publishing also moves the pack's version, and only publishing does. Saving does not, and neither does exporting: a version says what players were given, and an afternoon of saving gives them nothing.\n\nIt moves on its own, by what actually changed since your last release. Something new — a character, a room, a conversation — moves the middle number. A change to something that was already there moves the last one. The first is yours alone: type it into the Version box when you decide a release is a new thing rather than more of the old one.\n\nA place of your own is next: it builds a room and puts a door to it in the bedroom you wake up in, and every tutorial after that goes through the same door.

[Tutorial: Putting things in the room]

# Tutorials: a tutorial's name
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.title = Putting things in the room

# Tutorials: the line under a tutorial's name
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.summary = Add objects to a place, layer them, and leave one switched off.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.roomMoreThanTwo.title = A room is more than two pictures

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.roomMoreThanTwo.body = The back and front layers are the room itself. Everything ELSE in it is a GameObject: its own picture, at its own position, with its own place in the stack — and, unlike the layers, something a dialogue or a rule can switch on and off while the game runs.\n\nThat is how a room changes. A door that opens is two objects, one switched off. A coat left on a chair is an object that appears once a conversation has happened. A lamp that comes on at night is the same trick again.\n\nObject art is NOT a level layer, so it is not 2048 by 1136. Draw it at whatever size the thing really is, on a transparent background; it is placed in the room rather than filling it.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.openRoomBuilt.title = Open the room you built

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.openRoomBuilt.body = This carries on in the same pack. Click your place in the list on the left — the one you made two tutorials ago, not a vanilla extension.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.openRoomBuilt.hint = Your places are the upper list; vanilla extensions are below it.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.addObject.title = Add an object

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.addObject.body = Use + Add GameObject. It arrives empty and unnamed, which is fine — the next step is what makes it a thing.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.addObject.hint = + Add GameObject, under the GameObjects box.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.giveNamePicture.title = Give it a name and a picture

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.giveNamePicture.body = The name is how everything else finds this object — a rule that switches it on names it, and names repeat all over a level, so pick something you would recognise months from now.\n\nFor the picture use TutorialArt/Locations/Vase.png. It is worth looking at before you pick it: it is a vase and almost nothing else, on a transparent background, at the size a vase actually is. Compare that to Room.png, which contains the same vase inside a full 2048 by 1136 room — the padding IS the difference between a layer and a prop. Art with a room's worth of empty space around it cannot be placed, only laid over everything.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.giveNamePicture.hint = Select the object in the tree, then fill in Name and its sprite.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.putWhereWant.title = Put it where you want it

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.putWhereWant.body = Drag the object in the preview. The gizmo moves the real position — this is not a preview-only control, it is the same X and Y you could type in by hand, and typing is the fallback when you want an exact number rather than a look.\n\nPut the vase somewhere it could plausibly stand. It will be drawing over the whole room at the moment, which the next step fixes.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.putWhereWant.hint = Click the object in the preview, then drag it.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.decideStandsFront.title = Decide what it stands in front of

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.decideStandsFront.body = Sorting order is the stack. The back layer sits at -12 and the front layer at -10, so an object at -11 stands BETWEEN them: behind the furniture in the front layer, in front of the wall behind it. Anything above -10 draws over the whole room.\n\nA new object starts at 0, which is over everything. Set it to -11 and watch the preview put it into the room rather than on top of it.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.decideStandsFront.hint = Sorting order, on the selected object. -11 puts it between the layers.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.leaveSwitchedOff.title = Leave it switched off

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.leaveSwitchedOff.body = Untick Start active. The object is still in the room, at the position you gave it — it simply is not shown when the player arrives.\n\nThis is half of every change a room ever makes. The other half is a Set-Active action, from a dialogue node or an integration rule, naming this object. Build the object switched off now and the rule that reveals it has something to point at later.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.leaveSwitchedOff.hint = Start active, on the selected object. Untick it.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.previewTelling.title = What the preview is telling you

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.previewTelling.body = An object that starts switched off is drawn faded, so you can still position it — the game will draw nothing there until something turns it on. Fade objects that start inactive turns that off while you work.\n\nThe same goes for anything under a switched-off parent: the game draws none of it, so the preview fades all of it. If a whole group of your objects has gone pale, that is why.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.roomCanChange.title = A room that can change

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.dressingTheRoom.roomCanChange.body = You now have a room with something in it that is not part of the picture — placed, layered, and waiting to be switched on.\n\nObjects nest, so one can be a container for several and switching the parent moves all of them at once. And the Documentation section covers the rest of what a place carries: masks, weather, and the beach ambience a room can keep or drop.

[Tutorial: On the world map]

# Tutorials: a tutorial's name
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.title = On the world map

# Tutorials: the line under a tutorial's name
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.summary = Put a place on the world map so a player can travel to it directly.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.twoWaysReachRoom.title = Two ways to reach a room

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.twoWaysReachRoom.body = You have already built one: a navigator button on the bedroom's strip, which is a door from one room to another. It works, and it is the right shape for somewhere that sits BEHIND another place — a back office off a shop, a bedroom off a hall.\n\nThe world map is the other way, and it means something different. A place on the map is a destination in its own right rather than a room reached through another one.\n\nThe map is not open from everywhere, mind: the player reaches it by going to the Garage, into the Car, and pressing Drive. So a map button suits somewhere they would deliberately travel to, and a navigator button suits somewhere they walk into from next door. Most places want one or the other, not both.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.addMapButton.title = Add a map button

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.addMapButton.body = Use + Map button. It appears as a card in the list — the map buttons tab has no separate editor, each button IS its row.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.addMapButton.hint = + Map button, at the top of the tab.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.sayWhereGoes.title = Say where it goes

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.sayWhereGoes.body = Set Target place to the room you built. A button with no target is the quietest mistake in the editor: it saves, it exports, it appears on the map, and clicking it does nothing at all.\n\nValidate catches it, which is the reason to run Validate before every export rather than after something goes wrong.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.sayWhereGoes.hint = Target place, on the card you just added.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.chooseWhichMenuLives.title = Choose which menu it lives in

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.chooseWhichMenuLives.body = The world map is not one list of buttons — it is five radial menus, one per district: Seaside, The Line, Neon Row, Shopside and Foundry. District decides which one your button joins.\n\nA new button arrives in Foundry because it had to arrive somewhere. That is a default, not a decision. Pick the district your place actually belongs to — a player who opens the wrong menu will not find it, and nothing will tell them it exists.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.chooseWhichMenuLives.hint = District, on the same card. Any of the five except the one it started in.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.giveSomethingRead.title = Give it something to read

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.giveSomethingRead.body = Label is the text on the button. Write what a player would call the place, not what you called it in the editor.\n\nIt also accepts [PV:name], which is replaced with one of your pack's variables while the game runs — so a button can read "The Shop" before a conversation and "Anna's Shop" after one, without a second button.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.giveSomethingRead.hint = Label, on the same card.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.twoCanLeaveAlone.title = The two you can leave alone

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.twoCanLeaveAlone.body = Music switches the background track when the button is used, which is worth setting for somewhere with its own atmosphere and worth leaving empty otherwise — an empty Music keeps whatever was playing.\n\nConditions decide whether the button is shown at all. An empty list means always, which is what you want for now. Fill it in and the place stays off the map until the player has earned it — the same condition rows you will meet on dialogues and rules.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.somewhereGo.title = Somewhere to go

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.onTheWorldMap.somewhereGo.body = Validate, export, and open the world map in game: your place is in the district you chose, under the label you wrote.\n\nYou now have both routes — a door from the bedroom and a place on the map — and they are independent. Removing one does not affect the other, which is worth knowing when a place becomes reachable two ways by accident.

[Tutorial: Your first conversation]

# Tutorials: a tutorial's name
tutorial.firstConversation.title = Your first conversation

# Tutorials: the line under a tutorial's name
tutorial.firstConversation.summary = Write a dialogue that starts in your room, with a choice in it.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstConversation.dialogueTree.title = A dialogue is a tree

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstConversation.dialogueTree.body = Play runs down the node list from the top, and children are just nodes nested under a parent — reaching the end of a branch carries on to whatever is next in the list, not back out. Every node is one of three kinds. Text plays its line and moves on. Choice stops and offers its children to the player. Random picks one child itself. Everything else on a node — who speaks, what happens after, what it sets — hangs off that.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstConversation.addDialogue.title = Add a dialogue

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstConversation.addDialogue.body = Use + Dialogue. It needs a place to live in, which is why the room came first.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.firstConversation.addDialogue.hint = + Dialogue is in the toolbar above the list.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstConversation.sayWhereHappens.title = Say where it happens

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstConversation.sayWhereHappens.body = Set the level in the start conditions to the place you built. A dialogue with no level will never start, because nothing tells the game where to look for it.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.firstConversation.sayWhereHappens.hint = Start conditions, then the level row pinned at the top.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstConversation.writeLine.title = Write a line

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstConversation.restNodeBox.title = The rest of the Node box

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstConversation.restNodeBox.body = Actor is who speaks, and leaving it empty plays the line with whoever is already on screen. Expression and Outfit swap the bust mid-conversation — your practice character has neither, so leave them be. Tag names a node so a jump can find it. Duration decides whether the line waits for a click or times out on its own.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstConversation.givePlayerSay.title = Give the player a say

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstConversation.givePlayerSay.body = Add a second node, set its Kind to Choice, and hang two children off it with + Child. The Choice node's own Text is the prompt, shown under the options — it is what the player is answering. Each child IS an option, and the child's Text is the label on its button, not a line somebody says. Write all three: anything left blank shows up in game as blank, which is what an empty node looks like from the outside.\n\nGive the CHOICE node an actor too — its text is spoken, so it needs somebody to speak it. The children do not: an option is a button, not a line, and nobody says it aloud.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.firstConversation.givePlayerSay.hint = Set Kind to Choice, write its Text, + Child twice, then write each child's Text.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstConversation.happensAfterNode.title = What happens after a node

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstConversation.happensAfterNode.body = Jump decides where play goes next. Continue — the default — moves to the next node down the list, whether that is a child of this one or something further out. Exit stops the conversation and skips everything below. Jump resumes at whichever node carries the Tag you name.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.firstConversation.makeExitMeanSomething.title = Make Exit mean something

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.firstConversation.makeExitMeanSomething.body = At the very bottom of the list Continue and Exit are the same thing, because there is nothing left to skip either way. So give Exit something to skip: select the choice and add one more line beside it with + Sibling - the closing line - then set ONE of your two options to Exit. Take that option in game and the conversation stops; take the other and it carries on into the closing line.\n\nGive the closing line an actor as well. Every node that SAYS something needs one — a line with no speaker shows no name, which reads as a fault rather than as a narrator.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while

[Tutorial: Lines that choose themselves]

# Tutorials: a tutorial's name
tutorial.linesThatChoose.title = Lines that choose themselves

# Tutorials: the line under a tutorial's name
tutorial.linesThatChoose.summary = Gate a line on the state of the room, and let two speakers share a scene.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.linesThatChoose.notEveryLineShould.title = Not every line should play

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.linesThatChoose.notEveryLineShould.body = So far every node in your dialogue runs when play reaches it. A conversation that reacts to anything needs the opposite: lines that sometimes do not.\n\nThat is what a node's own Conditions box is for, and it behaves in two different ways depending on where the node sits. An ordinary node whose conditions fail is SKIPPED — play carries on to the next one. A node directly under a Choice is not offered at all: the player never sees that option, rather than seeing it greyed out.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.linesThatChoose.openConversationWrote.title = Open the conversation you wrote

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.linesThatChoose.openConversationWrote.body = Same pack, same dialogue. Pick it in the list, then select any node in the tree — the one you want the condition on.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.linesThatChoose.openConversationWrote.hint = Click the dialogue, then a node in the list beside it.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.linesThatChoose.gateSomethingReal.title = Gate it on something real

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.linesThatChoose.gateSomethingReal.body = Add a condition to that node with + Add condition, then finish it — an empty condition row is not a gate, it is a blank that always passes.\n\nSet its Type to GameObjectActive. The row then asks the same three things in the same order the Set-Active action asks them: Category, Level, Target. That is deliberate — a condition reads back exactly what that action sets, so it addresses the object the same way.\n\nSet Category to GameObjects, since the object lives inside a place. Set Level to your place: the Target dropdown stays disabled until you do, because it lists that level's objects and nothing else. Then pick the object you put in the room and left switched off.\n\nDoing this against something you already built matters. The object is genuinely off, so the line genuinely will not play — and when a rule switches the object on later, the line starts appearing on its own. The conversation is reading the state of the room.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.linesThatChoose.gateSomethingReal.hint = Type = GameObjectActive, then Category, Level and Target below it.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.linesThatChoose.conditionsDoNotStop.title = Conditions do not stop at objects

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.linesThatChoose.conditionsDoNotStop.body = The same box offers everything the pack can ask about: which place is on screen, what a variable holds, whether it is raining, a percentage rolled once a day. Every condition in the list has to pass, and an empty list always passes — which is why a node with no conditions always plays.\n\nAny condition can also be negated, which is usually shorter than writing the opposite one.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.linesThatChoose.someoneElseRoom.title = Someone else in the room

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.linesThatChoose.someoneElseRoom.body = A conversation is rarely one voice. The Actor field on a node says who speaks it, and it holds from that node onward until another one changes it — you do not set it per line.\n\nEvery pack has a speaker it did not create: the player. Add a node and set its Actor to the player, and the line is the player talking back. Any mod addressing you reaches that same character, which is why its name and colour are fixed and yours to use rather than define.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.linesThatChoose.someoneElseRoom.hint = Add a node, write a line, then set Actor to player.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.linesThatChoose.lettingOneOptionSay.title = Letting one option say more

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.linesThatChoose.lettingOneOptionSay.body = Last tutorial you gave one option Exit and let the other fall through to your closing line. Both are still one line long. Real dialogue is lopsided — one answer earns a reaction, the other does not — and the branch that reacts still has to end up somewhere, or you write the ending twice.\n\nA TAG is a name you give a node so another node can send play to it. Two fields do it. Tag, on the node being aimed AT - tick it to give the node one: a short word, yours to choose, and it is a label rather than anything the player sees. Then, on the node doing the aiming: set it to Jump, and a Jump to box appears listing the tags in this dialogue.\n\nBuild it in that order — the tag first, so it is there to be picked. Tag your closing line, the one you added last tutorial, with something like ending. Then take the option you did NOT set to Exit, add a Child under it, and write the reaction that answer deserves. On that child set Then to Jump, and choose ending in the Jump to box.\n\nPlay now runs the option, the reaction, and then lands on the closing line. The other option still ends where it ended. One ending, written once, reached two ways — and nothing repeats, because every jump here goes forward.

# Tutorials: the nudge shown when a step has been waiting a while
tutorial.linesThatChoose.lettingOneOptionSay.hint = Tag the closing line, then + Child on the non-Exit option, set its Then to Jump and pick that tag.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.linesThatChoose.jumpingBackwardsPurpose.title = Jumping backwards on purpose

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.linesThatChoose.jumpingBackwardsPurpose.body = Forward is not the only direction, and backwards is not a mistake. Jumping back to a Choice is one of the most useful shapes there is, and the game itself is full of it: a menu where each option answers and then returns, except one that carries the conversation on. Ask about the weather, come back. Ask about her sister, come back. Say you should get going, and that one continues.\n\nTo build it, tag the Choice node itself, then give the last line of each returning branch a jump to that tag. The option that leaves simply does not jump — it continues, or exits.\n\nThe one thing to be sure of is a way out. If every option comes back, the player cannot leave; at least one has to not return. Put that option in the menu from the start rather than behind a condition, or a player who fails the condition is stuck in a conversation with no exit.\n\nAnd give a tag to exactly one node. Two nodes carrying the same tag make every jump aimed at it ambiguous: play goes to whichever the game reaches first, which is not something you chose and may not stay the same.

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.linesThatChoose.conversationMemoryRoom.title = A conversation with a memory of the room

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.linesThatChoose.conversationMemoryRoom.body = Your dialogue now has a line that only plays when the room is in a particular state, a second speaker, and a branch that rejoins.\n\nWhat it still cannot do is remember anything across visits — the room's state is the room's, not the conversation's. That is what variables are for, and they are the next group.

[Tutorial: A face that moves]

tutorial.aFaceThatMoves.title = A face that moves

# Tutorials: the heading of a step
tutorial.aFaceThatMoves.bustStackPictures.title = A bust is a stack of pictures

# Tutorials: what the step says
tutorial.aFaceThatMoves.bustStackPictures.body = The base sprite is the whole character. Everything else is a small picture laid over the same 256 by 256 frame, in the same place, swapped in when the game wants it.\n\nThere are three kinds. A BLINK frame is the eyes closed, shown for a fifth of a second every few seconds. Four MOUTH frames cycle while a line types, so the character looks like they are speaking. Four EXPRESSIONS — Happy, Angry, Sad and Flirty — are swapped in by a dialogue line and stay until something changes them.\n\nEach is drawn on a transparent background at the same size as the base, so it lines up. Draw only the part that changes: for a blink, that is a pair of closed eyes and nothing else.
